AI Factory Case Studies · Part 2 · Stargate Abilene

Stargate Abilene: The AI Factory Built on Other People's Money

xAI built Colossus itself. OpenAI's flagship campus in Abilene, Texas was built by a chain of companies: a landowner, a developer, private-equity investors, banks and a cloud provider, all betting on one customer. This case study follows that chain, the eight buildings it is paying for, the gas turbines behind the meter, and what the model means for who carries the risk if AI demand falls short.

3. The bet: split the factory into layers others will finance

No single company in this chain could easily have paid for a 1.2 GW campus on its own balance sheet in 2024. OpenAI was a fast-growing startup, Crusoe was a former bitcoin-mining energy company, and Oracle was already borrowing heavily. The solution was to split the factory into layers and give each layer to whoever was willing to own it: land and power to Lancium, the buildings to a joint venture financed with private equity and bank loans, the computers and operations to Oracle, and the demand to OpenAI.

💡 Why this mattersSplitting the factory turns a frontier lab's compute need into something investors already know how to fund: a real-estate project with a long lease from a creditworthy tenant. It unlocks far more money, far faster. It also means every layer depends on the one below it being paid, and in the end on OpenAI's revenue.

Who owns what

5. The money

The financing came in two phases. In October 2024 Crusoe, Blue Owl Capital and Primary Digital Infrastructure formed a $3.4 billion joint venture for the first phase, two buildings of about 200 MW. A deal-tracking site lists a $2.3 billion J.P. Morgan loan closing in January 2025 at the Phase 1 address ⚠️. In May 2025 the second phase, adding six buildings, closed as part of a $15 billion joint venture, including a $7.1 billion construction loan from a consortium led by J.P. Morgan, arranged by Newmark. DCD reported Crusoe securing $11.6 billion of debt and equity for the campus.

The two phases of financing

Announced amounts, in billions of dollars. These figures overlap and should not be added together: the $15 billion is the total JV for the campus, and the loans sit inside it.

Sources: Paul Hastings and Kirkland & Ellis deal releases (Oct 2024, May 2025), Newmark via Converge Digest, DCD, traded.co ⚠️.

On top of the buildings sits a bigger commitment: Oracle's reported multi-year agreement to provide OpenAI with compute across several Stargate sites, which analysts value in the hundreds of billions of dollars. That agreement is what makes the building loans look safe to lenders, and it is why Oracle's own debt has drawn scrutiny. Abilene is the first and most visible piece of it.

6. Eight buildings

Building tracker

Move the slider through time. Counts follow company statements as reported; the order of buildings is illustrative.

The campus has grown more slowly than first promised. When Phase 2 began in March 2025, the six new buildings were expected to go live by mid-2026. A June 2026 report noted the remaining buildings were still not online, and Epoch now expects the full campus in Q4 2026. An Epoch analysis and other trackers describe Stargate sites as taking longer and costing more than some competitors' builds. In March 2026 Oracle and OpenAI dropped plans to expand Abilene by about 600 MW, and the adjacent land went to a Microsoft campus of about 900 MW; DCD reported Meta was in talks for Crusoe capacity ⚠️.

7. Power and cooling

Abilene was chosen for its power. West Texas has abundant wind and solar, and Lancium's site was originally developed to soak up cheap renewable electricity for bitcoin mining. But a 1.2 GW AI campus needs firm power around the clock, so the campus also has its own gas generation. The September 2025 fact sheet describes a behind-the-meter gas microgrid using GE and Siemens turbines that can power the campus independently of the local grid. A permit change in January 2025 raised the allowed operating hours of each GE LM2500 turbine from 5,880 to 8,760 a year, which is every hour of the year ⚠️.

Power design: Colossus vs Abilene

For cooling, Abilene uses closed-loop liquid cooling with non-evaporative dry coolers. Water is filled once and recirculated, rather than evaporated in cooling towers, which matters in dry West Texas. The trade-off is more electricity for fans and chillers on hot days. Related reading: energy beyond the grid.

8. Community and incentives

Abilene's city council approved tax abatements of 85% on the taxable value of new improvements for 10 years, with separate agreements for each building so abatements can start as each is finished. The agreement requires Crusoe and Lancium to create 357 full-time jobs paying at least $57,600. Oracle is also eligible for an 85% property tax abatement through the city's economic development corporation, and Business Insider reported that Oracle is disputing the valuation of its site. Critics argue that a few hundred permanent jobs is a small return on billions of dollars of tax-free investment; supporters point to construction employment and a tax base that will grow as abatements expire.

⚖️ Compared with ColossusAbilene has not faced the permit fights that Colossus did: its turbines were permitted, it uses dry cooling and it sits away from dense housing. Its local controversy is about tax breaks and the number of jobs, not air quality.

VerdictAbilene shows how frontier compute became an asset class. By splitting one AI factory into land, buildings, cloud and customer, OpenAI and its partners raised more money than any of them had, faster than they could alone. The price is coordination, delays and a chain of companies all betting on the same customer. Next, Microsoft's Fairwater campuses show a third model: a hyperscaler building for itself and wiring its sites together.
